1) Answer

Short answer: There is credible evidence that Rishi Sunak has taken, endorsed, or preserved measures that protect human rights, even though some of his migration policies (notably the Rwanda scheme) were and are heavily contested by human rights institutions.

Key evidence that he values human rights:
- Direct engagement with Europe’s human-rights system: as Prime Minister he met the President of the European Court of Human Rights on 16 May 2023 and discussed “the importance of protecting human rights, democracy, and the rule of law throughout Europe.” ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/pm-meets-with-president-of-the-european-court-of-human-rights-16-may-2023?utm_source=openai))
- Using UK sanctions to defend rights abroad: his government joined US/Canada in a coordinated package on 8 Dec 2023 targeting individuals linked to abuses around the world, explicitly marking the Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ 75th anniversary; and in Oct 2022 sanctioned Iran’s “morality police” and senior security officials for serious violations. These are concrete measures against abusers, not just statements. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-and-allies-sanction-human-rights-abusers?utm_source=openai))
- Backing accountability for atrocity crimes: under Sunak, the UK hosted a major international war‑crimes meeting and boosted support to the International Criminal Court to pursue accountability for violations in Ukraine (20 Mar 2023). ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/london-hosts-major-international-war-crimes-meeting-as-uk-boosts-support-for-international-criminal-court?utm_source=openai))
- Preserving core domestic rights architecture: on 27 June 2023, his government confirmed in the House of Commons that it would not proceed with the Bill of Rights Bill (which would have replaced the Human Rights Act 1998). Whatever the political calculus, the practical effect was to leave HRA protections in place. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2023-06-27/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))
- Integrating rights language into wider tech governance: the UK’s international AI work (Seoul Summit) emphasized “human‑centric, trustworthy and responsible” AI to “protect human rights,” with the Prime Minister publicly backing that line. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/global-leaders-agree-to-launch-first-international-network-of-ai-safety-institutes-to-boost-understanding-of-ai?utm_source=openai))

Important counterpoints (for completeness):
- The Supreme Court ruled on 15 Nov 2023 that, on the evidence then available, removals to Rwanda posed a real risk of refoulement and were unlawful. Parliament later passed the Safety of Rwanda Act (Apr 2024) disapplying parts of the normal rights framework in these cases; the Council of Europe’s Human Rights Commissioner urged the UK not to remove people under the policy because of serious rights concerns. Sunak argued the policy could still be delivered within the UK’s obligations, but leading rights bodies disagreed. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: There is substantiated evidence that Sunak placed value on human rights in several domains (multilateral engagement, sanctions, accountability, retaining the HRA). At the same time, aspects of his migration agenda were judged incompatible with human‑rights protections by top courts and European rights institutions. Both sets of facts can be true: he advanced some rights‑protecting actions internationally while pursuing a highly contested approach to asylum at home.
